title: NULL and three-valued logic
summary: NULL means "unknown", not "empty". Any comparison with NULL yields unknown, which WHERE treats as false — the root of most NULL surprises, and the reason IS DISTINCT FROM and COALESCE exist.

examples.title: x <> 'a' doesn't match NULL; IS DISTINCT FROM does

annotations.note: brin's email is NULL, and NULL <> 'cay@example.com' evaluates to unknown, not true. WHERE keeps only true — so NULL rows vanish.
IS DISTINCT FROM treats NULL as a value you can compare: NULL is distinct from 'cay@example.com', so brin appears. It's the null-safe inequality.
COALESCE substitutes a display value for NULL. Don't use it to "fix" data in UPDATEs — store what you mean, render what you mean.

use_cases: Audit queries where 'not X' must include missing values (IS DISTINCT FROM / IS NULL)
strengths: Three-valued logic is mathematically consistent: unknown propagates honestly through AND/OR/NOT
IS DISTINCT FROM and IS NULL give you exact, index-friendly null handling
CHECK constraints treat unknown as pass, so partial data isn't rejected by mistake
weaknesses: Every predicate silently returns unknown on NULL: aggregates skip NULLs, NOT IN has its famous trap
NULL = NULL is not true, so joins and DISTINCT behave in ways SQL newcomers don't predict

pitfalls.title: NOT IN with a subquery that returns NULL
pitfalls.detail: x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) is never true: unknown compares kill the whole list. Use NOT EXISTS.

pitfalls.title: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col)
pitfalls.detail: COUNT(col) skips NULLs; COUNT(*) counts rows. Mixing them misreports totals.

pitfalls.title: Writing WHERE col = NULL
pitfalls.detail: Never true. NULL predicates are IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.

quiz.why: NULL <> 1 is unknown, and WHERE only passes true.

quiz.q: Which is the null-safe version of a <> b?
options: a != b OR a IS NULL
quiz.why: IS DISTINCT FROM compares with NULL-as-a-value in one expression, index-friendly and readable.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: Comparison Functions (IS DISTINCT FROM)

body:
## Concept

SQL has three logical values: true, false, and unknown. NULL compared to anything is
unknown, and WHERE-style filters keep only true. `IS NULL`, `IS DISTINCT FROM`
and `COALESCE` exist to handle unknowns deliberately.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- TS: null and undefined are values you can ===; SQL NULL is the *absence of a value*, and
  it isn't equal to itself. `NULL = NULL` is unknown, not true.
- Go: a NULLable column ≈ a pointer you must nil-check; the database forces the check in
  every predicate instead of panicking later.
- C: not a sentinel like NULL pointer dereference — it's a third truth value in the logic.

## Design notes

Schema design decides where NULL is meaningful: a missing value that means "not yet known"
earns NULL; one that means "none" deserves a real value (empty array, false, 0). Constraints
(NOT NULL) then encode the decision, so queries can rely on it. The NOT IN trap is an
anti-join lesson in disguise — covered properly with EXISTS in the joins module.

expected.three-values:
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 3
SELECT 1
    name
    ----
    ada
SELECT 2
    name
    ----
    ada
    brin
SELECT 3
    name | email
    -----+----------------
    ada  | ada@example.com
    brin | (no email)
    cay  | cay@example.com
